## Oliver's Research on Softball Pitcher Fatigue and Kinematics

The research examined kinematic variables such as center of mass (COM), trunk, and stride length during the first and last inning of a simulated game in youth softball pitchers. The study included thirty-two softball pitchers (12.4±1.6 years, 159.4±8.9 cm, 62.0±13.6 kg).

**Key Findings:**

A paired samples t-test revealed a statistically significant difference in trunk rotation during the first three pitching events from the first and last inning, with pitchers exhibiting less trunk rotation towards the pitching arm side. Trunk kinematics, stride length, and COM were altered as pitch volume increased, with trunk pathomechanics being indicative of poor trunk control and fatigue.

## Scapular Kinematics Research

Regarding scapular kinematics specifically, research measured scapular kinematics for high school female windmill softball pitchers to identify kinematic adaptations and changes in pitching performance due to fatigue. This was one of the first studies to analyze glenohumeral as well as scapulo-thoracic kinematics during this task, and found consistency in the glenohumeral, scapulo-thoracic and torso kinematics during the throwing protocol despite completing 105 pitches.

I've found several relevant results for your search. Here are the key findings:

## Overview

Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a rare and heterogeneous syndrome secondary to a compression of the neurovascular bundle in the thoracic outlet area. Muscle hypertrophy is recognized to induce vascular or neurogenic compression, especially in sports involving upper-arm solicitation.

## Incidence in Athletes

The incidence of TOS varies significantly between populations. In some populations, e.g., in certain groups of athletes, some sources report incidence rates as high as about 80 cases per 1000 people, while in the general population, it is equal to 2–4 per 1000.

## Systematic Review and Sport-Specific Findings

A systematic review published in 2022 by Garraud et al. examined TOS in sport. Baseball players, whose sport requires repetitive throwing motions, are at increased risk for arterial thoracic outlet syndrome in their dominant arm.

## Prognosis and Return to Sport

The prognosis of TOS in athletes seems to be better than in the general population, possibly due to their better physical condition and their younger age. One study demonstrated an 80% to 90% incidence of return to sport within 4 to 5 months in competitive athletes who presented with TOS and were aggressively treated.

I found several relevant studies on collegiate softball pitcher workload and pitch counts during tournament weekends. Here are the key findings:

## Pitch Counts During Tournament Weekends

A typical softball pitcher may throw between 1,200 to 1,500 pitches in a three-day weekend tournament.

## Research Findings on Workload and Injury Risk

Research has shown that pitchers report increasing fatigue and pain over a game and weekend tournament, and that the number of pitches thrown by pitchers varies widely. One study showed that pitchers throwing >85 pitches per game had an increased risk of injury over the season.

## Current Lack of Regulations

As of 2023, no established pitch count restrictions exist in the United States or Canada. No such recommendations exist for softball despite evidence showing that the underhand windmill pitching motion is not nearly as physiologically benign as once thought.

## Collegiate vs. Baseball Comparison

A notable difference exists in collegiate softball pitcher utilization compared to baseball pitchers, with fewer pitchers on softball teams leading to a higher cumulative workload per pitcher, including increased innings pitched per season, per game, and more game appearances.

## Research Needs

Further research, particularly at high school and collegiate levels, is needed.

# Summary of 4 Softball Pitching Biomechanics Articles

## Article 1
**Title:** Biomechanics of youth windmill softball pitching

**Authors:** Werner SL, Guido JA, McNeice RP, Richardson JL, Delude NA, Stewart GW

**Journal:** Am J Sports Med | **Year:** 2005 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 33(4):552-60

**DOI:** 10.1177/0363546504269253 | **PMID:** 15722291

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- "Shoulder distraction stress averaged 94% body weight for the youth pitchers"
- Study analyzed 53 youth softball pitchers
- "Vertical and braking force components under the stride foot were in excess of body weight"
- "Elbow and shoulder joint loads were similar to those found for baseball pitchers and college softball pitchers"

---

## Article 2
**Title:** Kinematics and kinetics of elite windmill softball pitching

**Authors:** Werner SL, Jones DG, Guido JA Jr, Brunet ME

**Journal:** Am J Sports Med | **Year:** 2006 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 34(4):597-603

**DOI:** 10.1177/0363546505281796 | **PMID:** 16282576

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- "Shoulder distraction stress averaged 80% of body weight for the Olympic pitchers"
- Study included 24 elite softball pitchers from 1996 Olympics
- "Sixty-nine percent of the variability in shoulder distraction can be explained by a combination of 7 parameters"
- Shoulder stress found "similar to that found in baseball pitchers"

---

## Article 3
**Title:** Biomechanics of windmill softball pitching with implications about injury mechanisms at the shoulder and elbow

**Authors:** Barrentine SW, Fleisig GS, Whiteside JA, Escamilla RF, Andrews JR

**Journal:** J Orthop Sports Phys Ther | **Year:** 1998 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 28(6):405-15

**DOI:** 10.2519/jospt.1998.28.6.405 | **PMID:** 9836172

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- Eight female fast pitch softball pitchers studied
- "Peak compressive forces at the elbow and shoulder equal to 70-98% of body weight were produced"
- "Shoulder extension and abduction torques equal to 9-10% of body weight x height were calculated"

---

## Article 4
**Title:** Biceps activity during windmill softball pitching: injury implications and comparison with overhand throwing

**Authors:** Rojas IL, Provencher MT, Bhatia S, Foucher KC, Bach BR Jr, Romeo AA, Wimmer MA, Verma NN

**Journal:** Am J Sports Med | **Year:** 2009 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 37(3):558-65

**DOI:** 10.1177/0363546508328105 | **PMID:** 19174551

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- Seven female windmill pitchers evaluated
- "Throws were of similar velocity (24 m/s, 53 mph)"
- "peak biceps brachii muscle activation during the windmill pitch was significantly greater than during the overhand throw when normalized (38% vs 19%)"

# Analysis of 4 Articles on Thoracic Outlet Syndrome and Softball

## Article 1
**Title:** "Nonunion of first rib fracture in a softball player: case report of a rare cause of thoracic outlet syndrome"

**Authors:** Young BL, Watson SL, Meyer RD, Ponce BA

**Journal:** J Shoulder Elbow Surg

**Year/Volume(Issue):Pages:** 2016;25(11):e353-e357

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jse.2016.07.025

**PMID:** 27742249

**Summary:** Case report describing one softball player with thoracic outlet syndrome caused by nonunion of a first rib fracture—presented as "a rare cause" of this condition.

**Softball mentioned:** Yes. **Number of softball athletes:** 1. **Pitcher status:** Not specified.

---

## Article 2
**Title:** "Occurrence, management, and outcome of thoracic outlet syndrome in a National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I conference"

**Authors:** Talutis SD, Ulloa JG, Hame SL, Gelabert HA

**Journal:** J Vasc Surg

**Year/Volume(Issue):Pages:** 2025;82(1):155-162

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jvs.2025.01.236

**PMID:** 40132734

**Summary:** Multi-sport epidemiologic study of 15,609 athletes (6,874 men; 8,735 women) over 7 years identified 76 TOS cases (0.48%): 7 venous TOS (9.2%) and 69 neurogenic TOS (90.8%). Tennis players showed 2.6% prevalence, softball 1.3%, rowers 1.3%. Most patients (96%) managed nonsurgically; 84.9% resolved with conservative treatment; 72.7% of 14.5% requiring surgery experienced symptom resolution. Overall 81.6% achieved symptom resolution; 95.4% achieved unrestricted return to competition.

**Softball mentioned:** Yes. **Number of softball athletes:** Approximately 10 (1.3% of ~776 athletes calculated from prevalence data). **Pitcher status:** Not specified.

---

## Article 3
**Title:** "Supracondylar process of the humerus causing brachial artery compression and digital embolization in a fast-pitch softball player. A case report"

**Authors:** Thompson JK, Edwards JD

**Journal:** Vasc Endovascular Surg

**Year/Volume(Issue):Pages:** 2005;39(5):445-448

**DOI:** 10.1177/153857440503900510

**PMID:** 16193218

**Summary:** First documented case of digital ischemia from thromboembolization caused by brachial artery compression from a supracondylar process (rare anatomical abnormality found in 0.4-2.7% of population).

**Softball mentioned:** Yes. **Number of softball athletes:** 1. **Pitcher status:** Yes—described as "fast-pitch softball player."

---

## Article 4
**Title:** "The impact of competitive level of high school and collegiate athletes on outcomes of thoracic outlet syndrome"

**Authors:** Talutis SD, Ulloa JG, Gelabert HA

**Journal:** J Vasc Surg

**Year/Volume(Issue):Pages:** 2024;79(2):388-396

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jvs.2023.10.061

**PMID:** 37931887

**Summary:** Retrospective comparison of 32 high school and 52 collegiate athletes (84 total). Females comprised 82.9% and 61.5% respectively. Primary diagnoses: venous TOS (50.0% vs 42.3%), neurogenic TOS (43.9% vs 57.7%). Baseball/softball comprised 39.3% of cases across both groups. Similar symptom resolution rates (80.0% vs 77.8%) and return-to-sport rates (72.4% vs 73.3%).

**Softball mentioned:** Yes (as baseball/softball combined). **Number of softball athletes:** Approximately 33 combined high school and collegiate athletes (39.3% of 84 total). **Pitcher status:** Not specified.

# Article 1

**Title:** A Narrative Review of Softball Pitching Workload and Pitch Counts in Relationship to Injury

**Authors:** Zaremski JL, Holtz K, Downs Talmage JL, Ulman S, Oliver GD

**Journal:** Sports Health

**Year:** 2025

**Volume(Issue):Pages:** 17(1):150-155

**DOI:** 10.1177/19417381241297160

**PMID:** 39584797

**Numeric Findings:**
- "One study showed that pitchers throwing >85 pitches per game had an increased risk of injury over the season."

---

# Article 2

**Title:** Effect of Pitching Consecutive Days in Youth Fast-Pitch Softball Tournaments on Objective Shoulder Strength and Subjective Shoulder Symptoms

**Authors:** Skillington SA, Brophy RH, Wright RW, Smith MV

**Journal:** American Journal of Sports Medicine

**Year:** 2017

**Volume(Issue):Pages:** 45(6):1413-1419

**DOI:** 10.1177/0363546516688657

**PMID:** 28298058

**Numeric Findings:**
- Sample: "Fourteen female fast-pitch softball pitchers between the ages of 14 and 18 years"
- Single day shoulder fatigue: "median, 2.0; 95% CI, 1.3-3.0"
- Single day shoulder pain: "median, 1.3; 95% CI, 0.5-2.3"
- Tournament shoulder fatigue: "median, 3.5; 95% CI, 1.5-5.5"
- Tournament shoulder pain: "median, 2.5; 95% CI, 1.0-4.5"

---

# Article 3

**Title:** Effects of a Simulated Game on Pitching Kinematics in Youth Softball Pitcher

**Authors:** Downs J, Friesen K, Anz AW, Dugas JR, Andrews JR, Oliver GD

**Journal:** International Journal of Sports Medicine

**Year:** 2020

**Volume(Issue):Pages:** 41(3):189-195

**DOI:** 10.1055/a-1062-6475

**PMID:** 31905407

**Numeric Findings:**
- Sample: "Thirty-two youth softball pitchers (12.4±1.6 years, 159.4±8.9 cm, 62.0±13.6 kg)"
- Stride length correlation: "r=0.367, p=0.039"
- Center of mass correlation: "r=0.364, p=0.041"
- Trunk flexion correlations: "r=-0.392, p=0.026" through "r=-0.436, p=0.013"

---

# Article 4

**Title:** Pitch counts and overuse in high school softball pitchers: a pilot study encompassing bullpen, warm-up, and game pitches

**Authors:** Kamarajugadda S, Pazik M, Horodyski M, Farmer K, Zaremski J, Zeppieri G, Roach R, Prine B, Moser M, Smith MS

**Journal:** Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness

**Year:** 2025

**Volume(Issue):Pages:** 65(10):1306-1310

**DOI:** 10.23736/S0022-4707.25.16806-0

**PMID:** 40673787

**Numeric Findings:**
- Total pitches counted: "8248 pitches...during 89 varsity high school fastpitch softball pitcher outings"
- Game-only above recommendation: "25.6% of pitchers pitched above the recommendation"
- Including bullpen/warm-up above recommendation: "increased to 51.2%"
- Statistical significance: "P=0.001"

# Article Citations and Key Findings

## Article 1
**Title:** "Descriptive epidemiology of collegiate women's softball injuries: National Collegiate Athletic Association Injury Surveillance System, 1988-1989 through 2003-2004"

**Authors:** Marshall SW, Hamstra-Wright KL, Dick R, Grove KA, Agel J

**Journal:** J Athl Train | **Year:** 2007 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 42(2):286-94

**DOI:** Not provided | **PMID:** 17710178

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- "preseason practice injury rates were more than double the regular-season practice injury rates (3.65 versus 1.68 injuries per 1000 athlete-exposures)"
- "The rate of injury in a game was 1.6 times that in a practice (4.30 versus 2.67 injuries per 1000 athlete-exposures)"
- "51.2% of game injuries resulted from 'other-contact' mechanisms, whereas 55% of practice injuries resulted from noncontact mechanisms"
- "ankle ligament sprains and knee internal derangements accounted for 19% of injuries" (games)
- "Twenty-three percent of all game injuries were due to sliding"

---

## Article 2
**Title:** "Epidemiology of Injuries in National Collegiate Athletic Association Women's Softball: 2014-2015 Through 2018-2019"

**Authors:** Veillard KL, Boltz AJ, Robison HJ, Morris SN, Collins CL, Chandran A

**Journal:** J Athl Train | **Year:** 2021 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 56(7):734-741

**DOI:** 10.4085/1062-6050-668-20 | **PMID:** 34280289

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- "The overall injury rate was 3.92 per 1000 athlete exposures"
- "Most injuries were shoulder (15.2%), hand/wrist (11.8%), knee (11.2%), and head/face injuries (11.2%)"
- "were classified as contusions (14.2%), sprains (14.1%), and inflammatory conditions (14.1%)"
- "Concussion (6.8%) was the most commonly reported injury"

---

## Article 3
**Title:** "Incidence of injuries in high school softball and baseball players"

**Authors:** Shanley E, Rauh MJ, Michener LA, Ellenbecker TS

**Journal:** J Athl Train | **Year:** 2011 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 46(6):648-54

**DOI:** 10.4085/1062-6050-46.6.648 | **PMID:** 22488191

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- "The overall incidence injury rate was 4.5/1000 athlete-exposures"
- "more injuries overall in softball players (5.6/1000 AEs) than in baseball players (4.0/1000 AEs)"
- "For both sports, the injury rate during games (4.6/1000 AEs) was similar to that during practices (4.1/1000 AEs)"
- "The incidence of injury for pitchers was 37.3% and for position players was 15.3%"
- "The upper extremity accounted for the highest proportion of injuries (63.3%)"

---

## Article 4
**Title:** "Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Sport: A Systematic Review"

**Authors:** Garraud T, Pomares G, Daley P, Menu P, Dauty M, Fouasson-Chailloux A

**Journal:** Front Physiol | **Year:** 2022 | **Volume(Issue):Pages:** 13:838014

**DOI:** 10.3389/fphys.2022.838014 | **PMID:** 35755427

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- "Seventy-eight articles were selected including 40 case reports, 10 clinical studies and 28 reviews of literature"
- "Baseball pitchers seem to be highly at risk of developing a TOS"

The NCAA doesn't have a hard cap on the number of pitches a pitcher can throw in a single game. This is a significant difference from baseball, where pitch counts are strictly regulated.

I found the research you were looking for. The study by Patrick Albright and colleagues examined pitch count and rest time guidelines in baseball and softball. 

The research highlights that while pitch count and rest time guidelines are widely employed in youth baseball to mitigate injury risk, similar recommendations are lacking in youth softball, despite evidence of potential overuse injuries from the underhand windmill pitching motion.

A key finding is that collegiate softball and baseball rosters differ significantly, with softball teams typically featuring fewer pitchers, which may lead to increased pitching demands for individual softball pitchers, potentially exacerbating injury risks.

Notably, only 7.35% of collegiate baseball pitchers throw over 100 innings in a season, compared with a much larger proportion (43%) of softball pitchers, and softball pitchers tend to have significantly more NCAA game appearances and innings pitched per season compared to baseball.

The full article is published in the Journal of Women's Sports Medicine and examines data from NCAA Division I softball and baseball College World Series teams from 2016 through 2021.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the Zaremski narrative review on softball pitching workload:

The article "A Narrative Review of Softball Pitching Workload and Pitch Counts in Relationship to Injury" was published in Sports Health in 2025 (January-February), authored by Jason L. Zaremski and colleagues.

Regarding the 1200-1500 pitches in weekend tournaments, over a three-day tournament a starting softball pitcher can throw on average 1200 to 1500 pitches compared to 100 to 150 for baseball pitchers.

Key findings from the narrative review include:

- Research has shown that pitchers report increasing fatigue and pain over a game and weekend tournament, and that the number of pitches thrown by pitchers varies widely

- One study showed that pitchers throwing >85 pitches per game had an increased risk of injury over the season

- As of 2023, no established pitch count restrictions exist in the United States or Canada

The review emphasizes that softball pitchers are at an increased risk of overuse injury and further research is needed to recommend specific workload interventions such as pitch counts.

# Softball Pitching Workload: Key Findings

## (1) Tournament Pitch Counts Comparison
"In a weekend tournament, the average pitcher can throw anywhere from 95 to 381 pitches." The document notes that collegiate softball pitchers throw significantly more innings per season (43% exceed 100 innings) compared to baseball pitchers (only 7.35% exceed 100 innings).

## (2) >85 Pitches Per Game Injury Risk
"softball pitchers throwing >85 pitches per game are more than twice as likely to seek medical attention for an injury and play through pain over the course of the season." This finding is cited to Gooch et al., 2022 (reference 22).

## (3) Pitch Count Restrictions Status
"As of 2023, there are no established pitch count restrictions in place for USA Softball or the National Federation of State High School Associations." Regarding NCAA: "There are also no established pitch count guidelines for collegiate softball." However, NCAA limits practice to "4 hours per day or 20 hours per week" during season, with one guaranteed day off weekly.

## (4) Pitch/Inning Numbers
- Youth/high school pitchers with pain: ~429 pitches/week
- Those without pain: ~219 pitches/week
- Professional injured pitchers: 967 more pitches/season than non-injured

## (5) Consecutive-Day and Year-Round Play
"middle-school-aged softball pitchers who compete year-round without adequate offseason rest are significantly more likely to experience reduced stamina and multiple overuse injuries." Youth pitchers showed "increased shoulder fatigue, pain, and weakness when pitching on consecutive days during a weekend tournament."

# Article Summary with Numeric Findings

## Article 1
**Title:** Effects of a Simulated Game and Doubleheader Inning on Peak Kinetics in Softball Pitching Across Pitch Types

**Authors:** Fava AW, Downs Talmage JL, van Hogerwou T, Oliver GD

**Journal:** American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2024, 52(12):3118-3129

**DOI:** 10.1177/03635465241278359 | **PMID:** 39344907

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- Study population: "19 high school softball pitchers (mean age, 15.1 ± 1.5 years; mean height, 1.6 ± 0.2 m; mean weight, 76.3 ± 16.9 kg)"
- Pitch protocol: "4 innings of 25 randomly assigned pitches"
- Rest period: "30 minutes" between simulated game and doubleheader
- Statistical significance thresholds: "P < .016" and "P < .008"
- Findings: "significant decreases in kinetics were observed at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist in the last and doubleheader innings"

---

## Article 2
**Title:** Decreased Shoulder and Elbow Joint Loads During the Changeup Compared With the Fastball and Curveball in NCAA Division I Collegiate Softball Pitchers

**Authors:** Oliver GD, Downs Talmage JL, Friesen KB, Saper MG, Dugas JR

**Journal:** Orthopedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 2021, 9(9):23259671211026625

**DOI:** 10.1177/23259671211026625 | **PMID:** 34527754

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- Study population: "27 female NCAA Division I softball pitchers (age, 20.2 ± 1.9 years; height, 175.7 ± 5.7 cm; weight, 83.6 ± 12.7 kg)"
- Pitch protocol: "3 balls of each pitch type"
- Statistical results: "Wilks λ = .087; F = 36.523; P < .001"
- Pitch type comparisons showed "P < .001" and "P = .012" differences
- Finding: "pitch speed between all 3 pitch types" showed "P = .006" significance

---

## Article 3
**Title:** Performance Demands in Softball Pitching: A Comprehensive Muscle Fatigue Study

**Authors:** Corben JS, Cerrone SA, Soviero JE, Kwiecien SY, Nicholas SJ, McHugh MP

**Journal:** American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2015, 43(8):2035-41

**DOI:** 10.1177/0363546515588179 | **PMID:** 26109610

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- Study population: "19 female softball pitchers (mean age [±SD], 15.2 ± 1.2 years)"
- Performance metrics: "mean number of pitches, 99 ± 21; mean innings pitched, 5 ± 1"
- "mean (±SD) pitch velocity was 49 ± 4 mph"
- Fatigue results by region:
  - Hip: "dominant, 19.3%; nondominant, 15.2%"
  - Scapular: "dominant, 19.2%; nondominant, 19.3%"
  - Shoulder: "dominant, 16.9%; nondominant, 11.6%"
  - Elbow flexors: "dominant, 22.5%; nondominant, 19.2%"
  - Wrist flexors: "dominant, 21.6%; nondominant, 19.0%"
  - Supinators: "dominant, 21.8%; nondominant, 15.5%"
  - Elbow extensors: "dominant, 22.1%; nondominant, 11.3%"
- Velocity change: "3.4% ± 5.0%, P < .01" from first to last inning

---

## Article 4
**Title:** Low-Cost Lower Extremity Screening to Predict Shoulder Distraction Force in College Softball Pitchers

**Authors:** Ulman SM, Nebel AR, Bordelon NM, Oliver GD

**Journal:** American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2025, 53(3):565-570

**DOI:** 10.1177/03635465241310243 | **PMID:** 39844736

**Key Numeric Findings:**
- Study population: "46 collegiate softball pitchers (mean age, 19.8 ± 1.1 years; mean height, 1.7 ± 0.1 m; mean weight, 78.9 ± 11.9 kg)"
- Null model prediction: "significantly predicted peak shoulder distraction force (P < .001), accounting for 49.9% of the variance"
- Hip rotation strength contribution: "P = .015" with "6.3% increase in variability accounted for (56.2% of the variance)"

Based on the search results, here's information about windmill softball pitch biomechanics:

## Pitch Phases

The 4 primary phases of the windmill softball pitch include the wind-up, stride, acceleration, and follow-through.

## Shoulder Motion and Abduction

The pitcher's arm moves from full elevation to 90 degrees of shoulder flexion and experiences full arm external rotation before releasing the ball following arm internal rotation and adduction across the body. One study mentions that the neutral position involves 90 degree abduction arm angle with the scapula forming a 30 degree angle anterior to the coronal plane.

## Forces and Torques at Release

Peak compressive forces at the elbow and shoulder equal to 70–98% of body weight were produced, and shoulder extension and abduction torques equal to 9–10% of body weight × height were calculated.

## Ball Release Position

Research has examined arm positioning at ball release. Some pitchers release the ball with the throwing arm tucked close to the trunk, while others let the arm float outwards in a more abducted position. The position of the arm at ball release may be key to the mechanism of shoulder pain.

Based on the search results, I found the information you're looking for. This research comes from a 2022 study by Brittany Gooch and colleagues:

The study involved 28 female softball pitchers aged 14-18 years who completed an online survey about pitching history, pitch volume, and subjective reports of pain or injury in the back, shoulder, and elbow.

Chi-square analysis was used to compare those who pitched either >85 or <85 pitches per game with regard to frequency of shoulder pain, elbow pain, back pain, seeking of medical attention, and actual injury diagnosis.

The key finding was significant: Those with pitch counts of >85/game were more than twice as likely to see a physician regarding pain/injury.

Additionally, weekly and yearly pitch counts were higher in those reporting pain or injury in the shoulder and back, with pitchers reporting pain throwing around 429 pitches per week versus 219 pitches per week for those without pain.

# Study Citation & Key Data

**Title:** "Shoulder and Scapular Kinematics during the Windmill Softball Pitch: The Effect of Fatigue"

**Authors:** Backus SI, Kraszewski A, Kontaxis A, Gibbons M, Bido J, Graziano J, Hafer J, Jones KJ, Hillstrom H, Fealy S

**Journal:** Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine | **Year:** 2013 | **Volume/Pages:** 1(4 Suppl):2325967113S00094 | **DOI:** 10.1177/2325967113S00094 | **PMID:** Not provided in excerpt

---

## Study Protocol Details

- **Pitcher Sample:** 8 female high school softball pitchers (no prior shoulder injury)
- **Fatigue Protocol:** 105 total pitches in sets of 15 with 5-minute rest intervals
- **Analysis Method:** Last five pitches of each set were averaged

---

## Kinematic Findings

The abstract reports that "ball speed and peak glenohumeral, scapulo-thoracic and thoracic angular rotations...were consistent across all sets," but **no specific numeric values for shoulder elevation angles, scapular upward rotation, retraction, or fatigue-related changes are provided** in the excerpt. The conclusion notes athletes "maintain shoulder kinematics and ball speed" despite 105 pitches, contrasting overhand pitchers who fatigue around 90 pitches.

I found several relevant research findings on shoulder injury prevention programs for pitchers. Here's what the evidence shows:

## Key Randomized Controlled Trial Evidence

Adolescent pitchers displayed clinically meaningful improvements in posterior shoulder flexibility and maintenance of their external rotation to internal rotation ratio during an Athletic Trainer supervised preseason program. Deficits in posterior shoulder flexibility and strength have been identified as modifiable risk factors for pitching injuries, and there are studies showing the effect of prevention programs on arm injuries and associated risk factors such as strength and range of motion.

## Effectiveness of Arm Care Programs

When implemented, arm care programs have been shown to be effective at reducing overuse injuries to the elbow and shoulder in overhead athletes, with one randomized controlled trial demonstrating a 48.5% reduction in elbow overuse injuries in youth baseball players. Additionally, stretching the posterior shoulder muscles lowered the incidence of shoulder and elbow injuries by 36% in high school baseball pitchers.

## Strength Training Approaches

External rotation muscle strength training was not inferior to sleeper stretching for the prevention of shoulder and elbow injuries in high school baseball players. This was the first prospective study to provide evidence that external rotation muscle strength training is effective for preventing shoulder and elbow injuries.

## Broader Program Evidence

The Thrower's Ten program was consistently associated with improvements in scapular stability, shoulder range of motion, rotator cuff strength, endurance, and sport-specific performance, with evidence supporting its feasibility in youth and team training settings.

External rotation muscle strength training was not inferior to sleeper stretching for the prevention of shoulder and elbow injuries in high school baseball players. This was the first prospective study to provide evidence that external rotation muscle strength training is effective for preventing shoulder and elbow injuries.

The Thrower's Ten program was consistently associated with improvements in scapular stability, shoulder range of motion, rotator cuff strength, endurance, and sport-specific performance, with evidence supporting its feasibility in youth and team training settings.

The study by Pletcher and colleagues, "The Influence of a Simulated Game on Muscular Strength in Female High-School and Collegiate Softball Pitchers," was published in Sports Biomechanics in 2021.

**Study Details:**

The study involved 14 softball pitchers (17.9 ± 2.3 years old) who completed baseline isokinetic strength assessments for knee, hip, trunk and pitching elbow flexion and extension as well as trunk rotation. Seven days later, participants pitched a simulated game consisting of 105 fastballs prior to repeating all strength assessments.

**Key Findings:**

Interestingly, the study found increases rather than declines in muscular strength following the simulated game. Stride leg knee extension peak torque was significantly higher post-simulated game (75.1 ± 24.6%BW) compared to baseline (64.0 ± 19.5%BW), and trunk flexion peak torque was significantly higher post-simulated game (84.8 ± 47.0%BW) compared to baseline (63.5 ± 47.1%BW).

However, the study notes that softball pitchers often pitch several games within a day and over consecutive days during competitive seasons, and high volumes of pitches thrown can decrease muscular strength, resulting in less proximal force generation and upper extremity compensation to maintain performance.

## NFHS Rule Requirement

NFHS Baseball Rule 6-2-6 requires each NFHS member state association to develop its own pitching restriction policy based on the number of pitches thrown during a game to afford pitchers a required rest period between pitching appearances. As of the 2017 high school baseball season, rules now require a pitching-restriction policy based on the number of pitches thrown in a game, replacing the prior innings limitation.

## State Association Implementation

Each National Federation of State High School Association (NFHS) member state association was directed to develop its own pitching-restriction policy based on the number of pitches thrown during a game and required rest days between pitching outings. The specific pitch limits and rest requirements vary by state association.

## Examples of State Policies

Different states adopted different thresholds. For instance, the maximum number of pitches is 105 pitches in a game, and pitchers have to have required days of rest whenever they throw at least 50 pitches, 75 pitches, or the maximum of 105.

## States Without Pitch Limits

Only two states that sanction baseball do not have pitch limits for 2017–Massachusetts does not follow National High School Federation rules for baseball and Connecticut has days of rest restrictions but no pitch limits.

The review analyzed **78 articles** (40 case reports, 10 clinical studies, 28 literature reviews), but the document does not provide a precise aggregate patient count across all studies.

**Baseball dominated significantly:** The authors note that "Baseball pitchers seem to be highly at risk of developing a TOS" and appear in the majority of case reports.

One series included "13 baseball players, 13 swimmers, 5 water polo players, four rowers and two volleyball players" (41 athletes total). Another series reported "47 baseball or softball players, 11 volleyball players, eight gymnasts and surprisingly only two swimmers" (97 N-TOS athletes).

**Softball cases:** The review mentions softball alongside baseball but provides **no discrete softball-only case count**. Softball appears grouped with baseball in the phrase "47 baseball or softball players."

## TOS Type Breakdown

The two major series showed different distributions:

- **Series 1 (N-TOS and V-TOS combined):** Baseball/swimmers heavily represented
- **Series 2 (N-TOS exclusively):** "47 baseball or softball players" among 97 athletes

The review notes that "83% of N-TOS, 12% of V-TOS and 3% of A-TOS" in a large surgical series of 1,431 patients, though this represented the general TOS population rather than athletes specifically.

# Article Summary

## Article 1
**Title:** "The influence of a simulated game on muscular strength in female high-school and collegiate softball pitchers"

**Authors:** Pletcher ER, Bordelon NM, Oliver GD, Lovalekar M, Gorse K, Nagai T, Connaboy C

**Journal:** Sports Biomech, 2024, 23(9):1210-1218

**DOI:** 10.1080/14763141.2021.1941229

**PMID:** 34134606

**Key Findings:** "Normalised (%BW) stride leg knee extension peak torque was significantly higher (p = 0.020) post-simulated game (75.1 ± 24.6%BW) as compared to baseline (64.0 ± 19.5%BW)" and "trunk flexion peak torque was significantly higher (p = 0.009) post-simulated game (84.8 ± 47.0%BW) as compared to baseline (63.5 ± 47.1%BW)."

---

## Article 2
**Title:** "Injury Prevention Programs for Throwing Injuries in Softball Players: A Systematic Review"

**Authors:** Paul J, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK

**Journal:** Sports Health, 2021, 13(4):390-395

**DOI:** 10.1177/1941738120978161

**PMID:** 33535878

**Review Scope:** Initial search identified 1605 articles; after filtering and screening, "7 articles remained and were included in the systematic review."

**Program Development Finding:** "Only 1 study detailed an injury prevention program for softball players."

---

## Article 3
**Title:** "Incidence of injuries in high school softball and baseball players"

**Authors:** Shanley E, Rauh MJ, Michener LA, Ellenbecker TS

**Journal:** J Athl Train, 2011, 46(6):648-54

**DOI:** 10.4085/1062-6050-46.6.648

**PMID:** 22488191

**Injury Rates:** The pitcher injury figures are **pooled data for both sports combined**. The text states: "The incidence of injury for pitchers was 37.3% and for position players was 15.3%," without differentiating between softball and baseball.

**Additional Findings:** "The overall incidence injury rate was 4.5/1000 athlete-exposures (AEs), with more injuries overall in softball players (5.6/1000 AEs) than in baseball players (4.0/1000 AEs)."

Freetly et al

Increased Utilization of Pitchers in NCAA Women's Softball
                   Compared to Men's Baseball

    Taylor Freetly, MD1, Patrick Albright, MD1, Sonali E Feeley2, Brian T Feeley, MD2, Caitlin Chambers, MD1
          1University of Minnesota Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Minneapolis, Minnesota, U.S.A.

  2University of California San Francisco Department of Orthopedic Surgery, San Francisco, California, U.S.A.

BACKGROUND: Pitch count and rest time guidelines are widely employed in youth baseball to mitigate
injury risk among pitchers. Similar recommendations are lacking in youth softball, despite evidence of
potential overuse injuries from the underhand windmill pitching motion. This disparity in regulation may
heighten injury susceptibility. Additionally, the composition of collegiate softball and baseball rosters
differs significantly, with softball teams typically featuring fewer pitchers. This discrepancy may lead to
increased pitching demands for individual softball pitchers, potentially exacerbating injury risks.
Therefore, understanding the relationship between the number of pitchers, game appearances, and injury
incidence is crucial for informing injury prevention strategies in both baseball and softball. We hypothesize
that individual softball pitchers will have significantly more game appearances per season and pitch more
innings per game and season as compared to baseball pitchers, and that softball rosters will average
significantly fewer pitchers per team than baseball rosters.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted of National Collegiate Athletic Association Division
I softball and baseball College World Series teams from 2016 to 2021. Individual data consisting of game
appearances and season innings pitched facilitated calculations for innings per game. Team data included
the number of athletes and pitchers per team. Statistical analysis comparing baseball and softball team
continuous variables utilized Student's t-test. Individual data, characterized by non-normal distribution,
was evaluated with the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney Test. A significance level of p < 0.05 was applied to all
analyses.
RESULTS: Softball pitchers had a significantly greater number of innings pitched per season (median 84.1
(21.0-143.2) vs 29.2 (10.0-56.1) p < 0.0001), game appearances per season (median 23.0 (10.0-32.0) vs 16.0
(9.0-21.0), p < 0.0001), and innings pitched per game (median 3.6 (2.2-4.7) vs 1.6 (1.1-2.8), p < 0.0001). Baseball
rosters averaged significantly more total players (35.7 � 3.9 vs 21.5 � 2.8, p < 0.0001), more pitchers (15.7 �
2.3 vs 4.5 � 1.1, p < 0.0001), and a greater percentage of their roster was made up of pitchers (44.2% � 6.4%
vs 21.0% � 4.4%, p < 0.0001).
CONCLUSION: This study highlights a notable difference in collegiate softball pitcher utilization
compared to baseball pitchers. Fewer pitchers on softball teams led to a higher cumulative workload per
pitcher, with increased innings pitched per season, per game, and more game appearances. While the
relationship between pitch count and injury risk is established in baseball, further research is needed to
understand its implications for softball pitchers.

content.content:
# Study 1

**Title:** Injuries to pitchers in women's collegiate fast-pitch softball

**Authors:** Loosli AR, Requa RK, Garrick JG, Hanley E

**Journal:** Am J Sports Med, 1992, 20(1):35-7

**DOI:** 10.1177/036354659202000110

**PMID:** 1554071

**Numeric Findings:**
- "26 injuries and complaints in 20 of 24 players"
- "15 grade I (nontime-loss) injuries"
- "6 grade II injuries (altered play)"
- "5 grade III (stopped play) injuries"
- "average of almost 7 weeks of time lost per injured player"
- "Eighty-two percent of the time-loss injuries (grades II and III) involved the upper extremity"

---

# Study 2

**Title:** Female collegiate windmill pitchers: influences to injury incidence

**Authors:** Hill JL, Humphries B, Weidner T, Newton RU

**Journal:** J Strength Cond Res, 2004, 18(3):426-31

**DOI:** 10.1519/1533-4287(2004)18<426:FCWPIT>2.0.CO;2

**PMID:** 15320672

**Numeric Findings:**
- "181 Division I (n = 45), II (n = 30), and III (n = 54) collegiate softball pitchers"
- "131 reported injuries, 36 were acute, 92 chronic/overuse, and 3 unspecified"
- "80 were directly from pitching, with 33 shoulder-related and 16 related to the lower back"
- "72.8% of surveyed pitchers being injured during the 2001-02 year"
- "109 took nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 140 used modalities, 11 received surgeries"

## KEY FINDINGS

### 1. TOS in softball — the scarcity, quantified
PubMed title/abstract search `"thoracic outlet"[TIAB] AND softball[TIAB]` returns **exactly 6 records**, all retrieved:
- **2 case reports in softball athletes** (Young 2016, N=1; Gibson 2021, N=1). Both are **structural/congenital first-rib pathology**, not repetitive-overhead overuse. **Neither identifies the patient as a pitcher.**
- **4 cohort/outcome studies where softball is pooled with baseball or given only as a prevalence** (Shutze 2017 n=44 pooled; Chandra 2014 n=13 pooled; Talutis 2024 39.3% pooled; Talutis 2025 softball 1.3%).

Searches for `Paget-Schroetter softball` and `effort thrombosis softball` return no softball-pitcher case at all; **Keller 2020's systematic review of PSS in athletes does not contain the word "softball" — zero softball effort-thrombosis cases in the systematic literature.** Garraud 2022's systematic review (78 articles) reports no discrete softball count.

**Net: no peer-reviewed paper attributes TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball pitcher to pitching.** Design ceiling across the entire softball TOS literature is the single case report (N=1).

The one usable collegiate number: **Talutis 2025 — softball TOS prevalence 1.3%** over 15,609 NCAA D-I athletes across 7 years, against a 0.48% all-sport rate. Softball sits above baseline but below tennis (2.6%). Outcomes are favorable: 96% managed nonoperatively, **95.4% returned to unrestricted competition**.

### 2. Windmill loads — magnitude matches baseball
| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Shoulder distraction, youth | **94% BW** | Werner 2005, n=53 |
| Shoulder distraction, elite/Olympic | **80% BW** | Werner 2006, n=24 |
| Peak compression, shoulder & elbow | **70–98% BW** | Barrentine 1998, n=8 |
| Shoulder extension/abduction torque | **9–10% BW × height** | Barrentine 1998 |
| Peak biceps activation, windmill vs overhand (velocity-matched) | **38% vs 19%** | Rojas 2009 |
| Scapular excursion through pitch | **5–22° per plane** | Holtz 2026, n=17 |

Three independent sources state windmill shoulder/elbow loads are **similar to baseball pitching** (Werner 2005, Werner 2006, Boden 2024; Minetos 2023 "comparable"). The underhand motion is **not** load-sparing — that is the central point for the brief. Rojas is the strongest single contrast: at matched ball velocity, biceps demand is **double** the overhand throw, consistent with the eccentric biceps-labral load at the bottom of the arc.

**6-o'clock / brush contact:** No retrieved study reports discrete kinetics for the brush-contact instant. Barrentine 1998 and Minetos 2023 place peak shoulder force in the **delivery phase**, which contains it. Werner 2006 found 7 parameters explained **69%** of distraction variance; Ulman 2025 showed **lower-extremity screening alone predicts 49.9%** of peak shoulder distraction, rising to **56.2%** with hip rotation strength — i.e. shoulder load in these pitchers is substantially driven by proximal mechanics, which is the actionable lever.

**Hyperabduction — INFERENCE, not measured.** The windmill carries the arm through full overhead elevation once per pitch, transiently and at high angular velocity. This differs from the *sustained* overhead posture implicated in swimming/volleyball TOS. **No windmill study reports maximum shoulder elevation angle or time spent above 90°.** The plausible outlet link is cumulative repetition (~100+ full arm circles per game, no rest rule), not sustained positional narrowing. Label this as inference in the brief.

### 3. Workload — the strongest part of the case
**Rules (verified):** **NCAA softball has NO pitch count limit and NO mandated rest.** Confirmed three ways: Zaremski 2025 states "no established pitch count guidelines for collegiate softball"; Freetly et al. Table 2 lists NCAA for **both** sports as "No restrictions / None" (citing the 2021–22 baseball and 2022–23 softball rulebooks); the NCAA softball playing-rules page lists no such document. **NCAA baseball likewise has no limit.** The contrast is at the level below: **NFHS Rule 6-2-6 (2017) requires every state association to adopt a baseball pitch-count restriction policy with mandated rest** (verified at nfhs.org; e.g. NC max 105 pitches/day). Per Freetly's Table 2 reading, NFHS softball is capped by *innings* (max 12 innings/day; 7+ in a day → 1 day rest), and most travel-ball organizations list **"No restrictions"** for softball.

**Collegiate workload (Freetly et al., 40 CWS teams per sport, 2016–21):**
- IP/season **84.1 vs 29.2** (2.9×)
- Appearances/season **23.0 vs 16.0**
- IP/game **3.6 vs 1.6** (2.3×)
- Pitchers per roster **4.5±1.1 (21.0%) vs 15.7±2.3 (44.2%)**
- **43.7% of softball pitchers exceed 100 IP/season vs 7.35% of baseball pitchers**

That roster structure *is* the one-pitcher-carries-the-staff pattern, quantified: a softball staff is under one-third the size of a baseball staff and each pitcher absorbs nearly 3× the innings.

**Volume thresholds (youth/HS only):** >85 pitches/game → **>2× likelihood of seeking medical attention** (Gooch 2022). Shoulder pain associated with **429 vs 219 pitches/week** and **19,195 vs 8,876 pitches/year**. HS game volume **61.8±31.5 pitches** (Shanley 2012). **Bullpen and warm-up pitches roughly double the count exceeding recommendations: 25.6% → 51.2%** (Kamarajugadda 2025) — the single most practically useful workload finding, since it is entirely invisible to game box scores.

**Fatigue — mixed direction, read carefully:**
- Corben 2015: after **99±21 pitches**, dominant-side deficits **11–22%** across hip, scapula, shoulder, elbow, wrist; **velocity −3.4%**.
- Fava 2024: kinetics **decreased** at shoulder, elbow, wrist in the last and doubleheader innings — the pitcher produces *less* force, not more.
- Downs 2020: trunk rotation, stride length and COM degrade with volume in youth.
- Pletcher 2024: stride-leg knee extension and trunk flexion strength **increased** post-105 pitches.
- Skillington 2017: consecutive-day tournament pitching raises fatigue (2.0 → 3.5) and pain (1.3 → 2.5).

Consistent reading: **proximal control and output degrade within and across days**, while isolated post-game strength tests can move either way. Do not present fatigue as a clean monotonic decline.

**Year-round/specialization:** Zaremski 2025 reports middle-school pitchers competing year-round without offseason rest are significantly more likely to have reduced stamina and multiple overuse injuries; Gooch's yearly volumes (up to ~19,000 pitches/yr) evidence the travel-ball exposure. No collegiate-specific specialization study surfaced.

### 4. Upper-extremity injury epidemiology
- **NCAA softball overall: 3.92 per 1,000 AE; shoulder is the #1 body part at 15.2%** (Veillard 2021).
- Game 4.30 vs practice 2.67 per 1,000 AE; **preseason practice 3.65 vs in-season 1.68** (Marshall 2007).
- HS: softball **5.6** vs baseball **4.0** per 1,000 AE; **UE = 63.3%** of injuries; pitchers 37.3% vs position players 15.3% (**pooled across both sports**) (Shanley 2011).
- **Collegiate pitchers specifically: 72.8% injured in one season (n=181)**, 92 of 131 injuries chronic/overuse, 33 shoulder-related (Hill 2004); **20 of 24 pitchers with injuries/complaints, 82% of time-loss injuries in the UE** (Loosli 1992).

**Categorization — important caveat:** the NCAA ISP codes by body part plus diagnosis category. **TOS and effort thrombosis are not separable fields**; a neurovascular case would be absorbed into "shoulder" or a general/medical category. **No TOS incidence can be derived from ISP data** — Talutis 2025's chart-review design is why it exists.

### 5. Prevention
There is effectively **no softball-specific prevention evidence**. Paul 2021's systematic review screened 1,605 articles, included 7, and found **only 1 described an injury-prevention program for softball players** — with no efficacy trial. Feeley 2024 offers recommendations (core/LE strengthening, fatigue monitoring) without testing them. Uptake is poor: **<46% of fastpitch coaches run any program** (Nurrenbern 2023), and **51% of youth pitching websites omit AOSSM guidance** (Coden 2025). Given Ulman 2025 (LE/hip screening predicts 49.9–56.2% of shoulder distraction variance), a lower-extremity/hip-driven program is the most evidence-aligned target, but it is **untested in softball**.

---

## EVIDENCE GAPS — where softball evidence does not exist

1. **TOS mechanism in softball pitchers: nonexistent.** Zero peer-reviewed cases attributing TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball pitcher to pitching. Any mechanistic claim must be extrapolated from baseball, and that extrapolation should be stated explicitly in the brief.
2. **Softball is systematically pooled with baseball** in every TOS cohort (Shutze, Chandra, Talutis 2024, Garraud). Only Talutis 2025 reports a softball-specific figure (1.3%) — and it gives no softball N, no venous/neurogenic split for softball, and does not identify pitchers.
3. **No peer-reviewed collegiate pitches-per-game or pitches-per-weekend figure exists.** Every pitch-count number in the literature is youth or high school. Collegiate workload is documented only in *innings and appearances* (Freetly). A program wanting a collegiate pitch count must measure it locally.
4. **Shoulder elevation angle and time above 90° during the windmill are unreported.** The hyperabduction-to-outlet-narrowing link cannot be supported with a number from any windmill study.
5. **NCAA ISP cannot yield a TOS or neurovascular rate** — no such diagnosis field.
6. **No pitcher-vs-position-player injury split in NCAA ISP softball data.** The 37.3%/15.3% split is high school and pools baseball with softball.
7. **No tested prevention program for softball pitchers.** The prevention RCT literature is baseball-only — Sakata 2019 (*AJSM*, ~48.5% reduction in elbow overuse injuries), Shitara 2022 (*Sci Rep*, ER strength training non-inferior to stretching), and the Thrower's Ten systematic review. **These were surfaced by search but NOT fetched/verified this session** — verify before citing.
8. **No fatigue or workload study has measured any neurovascular or thoracic-outlet outcome** in softball. The workload-to-TOS chain is mechanistically plausible but entirely unevidenced.

---

## COULD NOT VERIFY

- **"1,200–1,500 pitches in a 3-day tournament (vs 100–120 for baseball)."** This **does** appear in a peer-reviewed paper (Freetly et al., JWSM), but cited to **their reference 11 = Werner 2005**, a biomechanics study of 53 youth pitchers that reports **no tournament volume at all** — the citation does not support the figure. The only other peer-reviewed tournament figure, **95–381 pitches/weekend** (Zaremski 2025, ref 51 = Skillington 2017), is an **order of magnitude lower** and also describes **youth** pitchers. **Recommend the brief not use 1,200–1,500**, or use it only with this caveat attached.
- **Current NCAA rulebook text not directly retrieved.** The 2026–27 PDF returned ECONNRESET and the fs.ncaa.org PDF would not text-extract. The no-limit finding rests on Zaremski 2025, Freetly Table 2 (citing the 2021–22/2022–23 rulebooks), and the NCAA rules page listing no such document. Confirm against the current rulebook before publishing a rules claim.
- **Barrentine 1998 full text** — jospt.org returned 403 twice. All Barrentine numbers above come from the verified PubMed abstract. Phase-by-phase detail and any elevation angle were not obtainable.
- **Talutis 2025 softball case count.** Only the 1.3% prevalence is in the abstract; softball N and its venous/neurogenic split are not. (An earlier automated summary computed "~10 athletes" from an invented denominator — **discard that number**.)
- **AAP 2024 conference poster**, "Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in a Teenage Softball Pitcher" (16F, vascular TOS, first rib resection, symptom resolution) — **conference abstract, not peer-reviewed**. It is the closest thing to a softball-pitcher TOS case that exists; treat as anecdote.
- **Mayo Clinic News Network** (pitcher Brittany Rathbun, subclavian vein narrowing, rib resection) — **lay press, not evidence**.
- **Backus 2013 and Scarborough 2020** are **OJSM meeting-abstract supplements**, not full papers. Backus (8 HS pitchers, 105 pitches in sets of 15) reported ball speed and glenohumeral/scapulothoracic/thoracic rotations **stable across all sets** — contrasting overhand pitchers who fatigue near 90 pitches — but published **no numeric kinematic values**. Cite as abstract only.

---

## Bottom line for the brief
The softball-specific TOS evidence does not exist — say so plainly and extrapolate from baseball with the extrapolation labeled. What *is* strong, and what the brief should lead with, is the **exposure case**: windmill shoulder loads equal baseball's (80–94% BW distraction; biceps demand 2× at matched velocity), while collegiate softball pitchers throw **2.9× the innings on a staff one-third the size**, with **43.7% exceeding 100 IP/season**, under **no pitch count limit and no mandated rest at any level of the NCAA** — and roughly **half of true pitch volume is bullpen and warm-up that no one counts**.

## KEY FINDINGS

### 1. TOS in softball — the scarcity, quantified
PubMed title/abstract search `"thoracic outlet"[TIAB] AND softball[TIAB]` returns **exactly 6 records**, all retrieved:
- **2 case reports in softball athletes** (Young 2016, N=1; Gibson 2021, N=1). Both are **structural/congenital first-rib pathology**, not repetitive-overhead overuse. **Neither identifies the patient as a pitcher.**
- **4 cohort/outcome studies where softball is pooled with baseball or given only as a prevalence** (Shutze 2017 n=44 pooled; Chandra 2014 n=13 pooled; Talutis 2024 39.3% pooled; Talutis 2025 softball 1.3%).

Searches for `Paget-Schroetter softball` and `effort thrombosis softball` return no softball-pitcher case at all; **Keller 2020's systematic review of PSS in athletes does not contain the word "softball" — zero softball effort-thrombosis cases in the systematic literature.** Garraud 2022's systematic review (78 articles) reports no discrete softball count.

**Net: no peer-reviewed paper attributes TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball pitcher to pitching.** Design ceiling across the entire softball TOS literature is the single case report (N=1).

The one usable collegiate number: **Talutis 2025 — softball TOS prevalence 1.3%** over 15,609 NCAA D-I athletes across 7 years, against a 0.48% all-sport rate. Softball sits above baseline but below tennis (2.6%). Outcomes are favorable: 96% managed nonoperatively, **95.4% returned to unrestricted competition**.

### 2. Windmill loads — magnitude matches baseball
| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Shoulder distraction, youth | **94% BW** | Werner 2005, n=53 |
| Shoulder distraction, elite/Olympic | **80% BW** | Werner 2006, n=24 |
| Peak compression, shoulder & elbow | **70–98% BW** | Barrentine 1998, n=8 |
| Shoulder extension/abduction torque | **9–10% BW × height** | Barrentine 1998 |
| Peak biceps activation, windmill vs overhand (velocity-matched) | **38% vs 19%** | Rojas 2009 |
| Scapular excursion through pitch | **5–22° per plane** | Holtz 2026, n=17 |

Three independent sources state windmill shoulder/elbow loads are **similar to baseball pitching** (Werner 2005, Werner 2006, Boden 2024; Minetos 2023 "comparable"). The underhand motion is **not** load-sparing — that is the central point for the brief. Rojas is the strongest single contrast: at matched ball velocity, biceps demand is **double** the overhand throw, consistent with the eccentric biceps-labral load at the bottom of the arc.

**6-o'clock / brush contact:** No retrieved study reports discrete kinetics for the brush-contact instant. Barrentine 1998 and Minetos 2023 place peak shoulder force in the **delivery phase**, which contains it. Werner 2006 found 7 parameters explained **69%** of distraction variance; Ulman 2025 showed **lower-extremity screening alone predicts 49.9%** of peak shoulder distraction, rising to **56.2%** with hip rotation strength — i.e. shoulder load in these pitchers is substantially driven by proximal mechanics, which is the actionable lever.

**Hyperabduction — INFERENCE, not measured.** The windmill carries the arm through full overhead elevation once per pitch, transiently and at high angular velocity. This differs from the *sustained* overhead posture implicated in swimming/volleyball TOS. **No windmill study reports maximum shoulder elevation angle or time spent above 90°.** The plausible outlet link is cumulative repetition (~100+ full arm circles per game, no rest rule), not sustained positional narrowing. Label this as inference in the brief.

### 3. Workload — the strongest part of the case
**Rules (verified):** **NCAA softball has NO pitch count limit and NO mandated rest.** Confirmed three ways: Zaremski 2025 states "no established pitch count guidelines for collegiate softball"; Freetly et al. Table 2 lists NCAA for **both** sports as "No restrictions / None" (citing the 2021–22 baseball and 2022–23 softball rulebooks); the NCAA softball playing-rules page lists no such document. **NCAA baseball likewise has no limit.** The contrast is at the level below: **NFHS Rule 6-2-6 (2017) requires every state association to adopt a baseball pitch-count restriction policy with mandated rest** (verified at nfhs.org; e.g. NC max 105 pitches/day). Per Freetly's Table 2 reading, NFHS softball is capped by *innings* (max 12 innings/day; 7+ in a day → 1 day rest), and most travel-ball organizations list **"No restrictions"** for softball.

**Collegiate workload (Freetly et al., 40 CWS teams per sport, 2016–21):**
- IP/season **84.1 vs 29.2** (2.9×)
- Appearances/season **23.0 vs 16.0**
- IP/game **3.6 vs 1.6** (2.3×)
- Pitchers per roster **4.5±1.1 (21.0%) vs 15.7±2.3 (44.2%)**
- **43.7% of softball pitchers exceed 100 IP/season vs 7.35% of baseball pitchers**

That roster structure *is* the one-pitcher-carries-the-staff pattern, quantified: a softball staff is under one-third the size of a baseball staff and each pitcher absorbs nearly 3× the innings.

**Volume thresholds (youth/HS only):** >85 pitches/game → **>2× likelihood of seeking medical attention** (Gooch 2022). Shoulder pain associated with **429 vs 219 pitches/week** and **19,195 vs 8,876 pitches/year**. HS game volume **61.8±31.5 pitches** (Shanley 2012). **Bullpen and warm-up pitches roughly double the count exceeding recommendations: 25.6% → 51.2%** (Kamarajugadda 2025) — the single most practically useful workload finding, since it is entirely invisible to game box scores.

**Fatigue — mixed direction, read carefully:**
- Corben 2015: after **99±21 pitches**, dominant-side deficits **11–22%** across hip, scapula, shoulder, elbow, wrist; **velocity −3.4%**.
- Fava 2024: kinetics **decreased** at shoulder, elbow, wrist in the last and doubleheader innings — the pitcher produces *less* force, not more.
- Downs 2020: trunk rotation, stride length and COM degrade with volume in youth.
- Pletcher 2024: stride-leg knee extension and trunk flexion strength **increased** post-105 pitches.
- Skillington 2017: consecutive-day tournament pitching raises fatigue (2.0 → 3.5) and pain (1.3 → 2.5).

Consistent reading: **proximal control and output degrade within and across days**, while isolated post-game strength tests can move either way. Do not present fatigue as a clean monotonic decline.

**Year-round/specialization:** Zaremski 2025 reports middle-school pitchers competing year-round without offseason rest are significantly more likely to have reduced stamina and multiple overuse injuries; Gooch's yearly volumes (up to ~19,000 pitches/yr) evidence the travel-ball exposure. No collegiate-specific specialization study surfaced.

### 4. Upper-extremity injury epidemiology
- **NCAA softball overall: 3.92 per 1,000 AE; shoulder is the #1 body part at 15.2%** (Veillard 2021).
- Game 4.30 vs practice 2.67 per 1,000 AE; **preseason practice 3.65 vs in-season 1.68** (Marshall 2007).
- HS: softball **5.6** vs baseball **4.0** per 1,000 AE; **UE = 63.3%** of injuries; pitchers 37.3% vs position players 15.3% (**pooled across both sports**) (Shanley 2011).
- **Collegiate pitchers specifically: 72.8% injured in one season (n=181)**, 92 of 131 injuries chronic/overuse, 33 shoulder-related (Hill 2004); **20 of 24 pitchers with injuries/complaints, 82% of time-loss injuries in the UE** (Loosli 1992).

**Categorization — important caveat:** the NCAA ISP codes by body part plus diagnosis category. **TOS and effort thrombosis are not separable fields**; a neurovascular case would be absorbed into "shoulder" or a general/medical category. **No TOS incidence can be derived from ISP data** — Talutis 2025's chart-review design is why it exists.

### 5. Prevention
There is effectively **no softball-specific prevention evidence**. Paul 2021's systematic review screened 1,605 articles, included 7, and found **only 1 described an injury-prevention program for softball players** — with no efficacy trial. Feeley 2024 offers recommendations (core/LE strengthening, fatigue monitoring) without testing them. Uptake is poor: **<46% of fastpitch coaches run any program** (Nurrenbern 2023), and **51% of youth pitching websites omit AOSSM guidance** (Coden 2025). Given Ulman 2025 (LE/hip screening predicts 49.9–56.2% of shoulder distraction variance), a lower-extremity/hip-driven program is the most evidence-aligned target, but it is **untested in softball**.

---

## EVIDENCE GAPS — where softball evidence does not exist

1. **TOS mechanism in softball pitchers: nonexistent.** Zero peer-reviewed cases attributing TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball pitcher to pitching. Any mechanistic claim must be extrapolated from baseball, and that extrapolation should be stated explicitly in the brief.
2. **Softball is systematically pooled with baseball** in every TOS cohort (Shutze, Chandra, Talutis 2024, Garraud). Only Talutis 2025 reports a softball-specific figure (1.3%) — and it gives no softball N, no venous/neurogenic split for softball, and does not identify pitchers.
3. **No peer-reviewed collegiate pitches-per-game or pitches-per-weekend figure exists.** Every pitch-count number in the literature is youth or high school. Collegiate workload is documented only in *innings and appearances* (Freetly). A program wanting a collegiate pitch count must measure it locally.
4. **Shoulder elevation angle and time above 90° during the windmill are unreported.** The hyperabduction-to-outlet-narrowing link cannot be supported with a number from any windmill study.
5. **NCAA ISP cannot yield a TOS or neurovascular rate** — no such diagnosis field.
6. **No pitcher-vs-position-player injury split in NCAA ISP softball data.** The 37.3%/15.3% split is high school and pools baseball with softball.
7. **No tested prevention program for softball pitchers.** The prevention RCT literature is baseball-only — Sakata 2019 (*AJSM*, ~48.5% reduction in elbow overuse injuries), Shitara 2022 (*Sci Rep*, ER strength training non-inferior to stretching), and the Thrower's Ten systematic review. **These were surfaced by search but NOT fetched/verified this session** — verify before citing.
8. **No fatigue or workload study has measured any neurovascular or thoracic-outlet outcome** in softball. The workload-to-TOS chain is mechanistically plausible but entirely unevidenced.

---

## COULD NOT VERIFY

- **"1,200–1,500 pitches in a 3-day tournament (vs 100–120 for baseball)."** This **does** appear in a peer-reviewed paper (Freetly et al., JWSM), but cited to **their reference 11 = Werner 2005**, a biomechanics study of 53 youth pitchers that reports **no tournament volume at all** — the citation does not support the figure. The only other peer-reviewed tournament figure, **95–381 pitches/weekend** (Zaremski 2025, ref 51 = Skillington 2017), is an **order of magnitude lower** and also describes **youth** pitchers. **Recommend the brief not use 1,200–1,500**, or use it only with this caveat attached.
- **Current NCAA rulebook text not directly retrieved.** The 2026–27 PDF returned ECONNRESET and the fs.ncaa.org PDF would not text-extract. The no-limit finding rests on Zaremski 2025, Freetly Table 2 (citing the 2021–22/2022–23 rulebooks), and the NCAA rules page listing no such document. Confirm against the current rulebook before publishing a rules claim.
- **Barrentine 1998 full text** — jospt.org returned 403 twice. All Barrentine numbers above come from the verified PubMed abstract. Phase-by-phase detail and any elevation angle were not obtainable.
- **Talutis 2025 softball case count.** Only the 1.3% prevalence is in the abstract; softball N and its venous/neurogenic split are not. (An earlier automated summary computed "~10 athletes" from an invented denominator — **discard that number**.)
- **AAP 2024 conference poster**, "Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in a Teenage Softball Pitcher" (16F, vascular TOS, first rib resection, symptom resolution) — **conference abstract, not peer-reviewed**. It is the closest thing to a softball-pitcher TOS case that exists; treat as anecdote.
- **Mayo Clinic News Network** (pitcher Brittany Rathbun, subclavian vein narrowing, rib resection) — **lay press, not evidence**.
- **Backus 2013 and Scarborough 2020** are **OJSM meeting-abstract supplements**, not full papers. Backus (8 HS pitchers, 105 pitches in sets of 15) reported ball speed and glenohumeral/scapulothoracic/thoracic rotations **stable across all sets** — contrasting overhand pitchers who fatigue near 90 pitches — but published **no numeric kinematic values**. Cite as abstract only.

---

## Bottom line for the brief
The softball-specific TOS evidence does not exist — say so plainly and extrapolate from baseball with the extrapolation labeled. What *is* strong, and what the brief should lead with, is the **exposure case**: windmill shoulder loads equal baseball's (80–94% BW distraction; biceps demand 2× at matched velocity), while collegiate softball pitchers throw **2.9× the innings on a staff one-third the size**, with **43.7% exceeding 100 IP/season**, under **no pitch count limit and no mandated rest at any level of the NCAA** — and roughly **half of true pitch volume is bullpen and warm-up that no one counts**.
